sentences.zh: 傅玄

translations.literal: Fu Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan

sentences.zh: 傅玄，字休奕，北地泥陽人也。

translations.literal: Fu Xuan, style name Xiuyi, was a man of Niyang in Beidi.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan, whose courtesy name was Xiuyi, came from Niyang in Beidi commandery.

sentences.zh: 祖燮，漢漢陽太守。

translations.literal: His grandfather Xie was Han dynasty Prefect of Hanyang.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather, Fu Xie, had served the Han as prefect of Hanyang.

sentences.zh: 父幹，魏扶風太守。

translations.literal: His father Gan was Wei dynasty Prefect of Fufeng.
translations.idiomatic: His father, Fu Gan, was prefect of Fufeng under the Wei.

sentences.zh: 玄少孤貧，博學善屬文，解鐘律。

translations.literal: Xuan in youth was orphaned and poor, broadly learned and good at composing texts, and understood bells and musical pitch.
translations.idiomatic: Orphaned and poor in his youth, Fu Xuan nevertheless read widely, wrote well, and had a firm grasp of bells and musical temperament.

sentences.zh: 性剛勁亮直，不能容人之短。

translations.literal: By nature he was rigid, forceful, bright, and straight, and could not accommodate others' shortcomings.
translations.idiomatic: He was by nature stern, outspoken, and upright, and he had little patience for other men's faults.

sentences.zh: 郡上計吏再舉孝廉，太尉辟，皆不就。

translations.literal: The commandery's reporting clerk twice recommended him as Filially Pious and Incorrupt; the Grand Commandant summoned him; in each case he did not take office.
translations.idiomatic: The commandery's clerk on capital duty twice nominated him as filially pious and incorrupt, and the grand commandant summoned him to office, but he declined every time.

sentences.zh: 州舉秀才，除郎中，與東海繆施俱以時譽選入著作，撰集《魏書》。

translations.literal: The province nominated him as cultivated talent; he was appointed gentleman of the palace, and together with Mou Shi of Donghai, on contemporary reputation both were selected to enter the editorial office and compile the *History of Wei*.
translations.idiomatic: The province then recommended him as an outstanding scholar, and he received appointment as a gentleman of the palace. Together with Mou Shi of Donghai he was chosen, on the strength of his reputation, for the historiography office, where he helped compile the *History of Wei*.

sentences.zh: 後參安東、衛軍軍事，轉溫令，再遷弘農太守，領典農校尉。

translations.literal: Later he joined staff on military affairs for the General Who Maintains the East and the General Who Guards the Army, was transferred to be magistrate of Wen, twice promoted to governor of Hongnong, and concurrent colonel director of agriculture.
translations.idiomatic: He later served on the staffs of the generals who maintained the east and who guarded the army, became magistrate of Wen, rose twice to governor of Hongnong, and held the concurrent post of colonel director of agriculture.

sentences.zh: 所居稱職，數上書陳便宜，多所匡正。

translations.literal: Wherever he dwelt in office he was called competent; repeatedly he submitted memorials stating conveniences, and many things were corrected through him.
translations.idiomatic: In every post he earned a reputation for competence; he sent up memorial after memorial on practical reforms, and much of what he urged was put right.

sentences.zh: 五等建，封鶉觚男。

translations.literal: When the five ranks were established, he was enfeoffed as baron of Chungu.
translations.idiomatic: When the five-tier nobility was instituted, he was enfeoffed as baron of Chungu.

sentences.zh: 武帝為晉王，以玄為散騎常侍。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu was King of Jin, he appointed Xuan cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.
translations.idiomatic: While Emperor Wu was still king of Jin, he appointed Fu Xuan cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.

sentences.zh: 及受禪，進爵為子，加附馬都尉。

translations.literal: When [he] received the abdication, [Xuan's] noble rank was advanced to viscount, and he was additionally given chief commandant of attached cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: After the abdication, Fu Xuan's noble rank was raised to viscount, and he was also given the title of chief commandant of attached cavalry.

sentences.zh: 帝初即位，廣納直言，開不諱之路，玄及散騎常侍皇甫陶共掌諫職。

translations.literal: When the emperor first ascended the throne, he broadly accepted straight speech and opened a road on which nothing was taboo; Xuan together with cavalier attendant-in-ordinary Huangfu Tao jointly held the remonstrance duty.
translations.idiomatic: At the beginning of the reign the emperor welcomed blunt counsel and declared that nothing was off limits for remonstrance; Fu Xuan and the cavalier attendant-in-ordinary Huangfu Tao were jointly charged with that advisory role.

sentences.zh: 玄上疏曰：「臣聞先王之臨天下也，明其大教，長其義節。

translations.literal: Xuan submitted a memorial saying: "Your subject has heard that when former kings faced all under Heaven, they clarified their great teaching and extended righteousness and integrity."
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan presented a memorial that began: "I have heard that when the kings of old faced the realm, they made plain the great moral teaching and nurtured a sense of duty and integrity."

sentences.zh: 道化隆于上，清議行於下，上下相奉，人懷義心。

translations.literal: The way's transforming influence flourished above, pure discussion was practiced below, above and below mutually upheld one another, and people cherished a mind for righteousness.
translations.idiomatic: The transforming power of the Way flourished at court, while honest public opinion held sway in the countryside; high and low reinforced each other, and every man carried a sense of what was right.

sentences.zh: 亡秦蕩滅先王之制，以法術相禦，而義心亡矣。

translations.literal: The perished Qin swept away former kings' institutions, used statutes and methods to control one another, and the mind for righteousness was lost.
translations.idiomatic: The fallen Qin had torn down the institutions of the earlier kings, governed by legalist tricks and coercive technique, and in the process destroyed the moral conscience of the people.

sentences.zh: 近者魏武好法術，而天下貴刑名；

translations.literal: In recent times Emperor Wu of Wei favored statutes and methods, and all under Heaven esteemed punishments and names.
translations.idiomatic: In our own day Emperor Wu of Wei doted on legalist methods, and the empire learned to prize harsh law and clever nomenclature over everything else.

sentences.zh: 魏文慕通達，而天下賤守節。

translations.literal: Emperor Wen of Wei admired all-round penetration, and all under Heaven slighted holding to integrity.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen admired worldly sophistication, and the world came to despise men who clung stubbornly to principle.

sentences.zh: 其後綱維不攝，而虛無放誕之論盈於朝野，使天下無復清議，而亡秦之病復發於今。

translations.literal: Afterwards the net cords did not bind, and empty, wild, unrestrained discourse filled court and countryside, causing all under Heaven no longer to have pure discussion, and the malady of the perished Qin to break out again in the present.
translations.idiomatic: Discipline then collapsed, empty speculation and reckless talk flooded court and country, honest opinion fell silent, and the moral sickness that had destroyed Qin has broken out again in our time.

sentences.zh: 陛下聖德，龍興受禪，弘堯、舜之化，開正直之路，體夏禹之至儉，綜殷周之典文，臣詠歎而已，將又奚言！

translations.literal: Your Majesty, of sagely virtue—rising as a dragon and receiving the abdication—you spread Yao and Shun's transformation, open a road for the upright, embody Great Yu of Xia's utmost frugality, and compile the canonical texts of Yin and Zhou; your subject would only chant praise—what more is there to say!
translations.idiomatic: Your Majesty has risen with dragon virtue to accept the abdication; you have widened the influence of Yao and Shun, opened a path for the upright, embodied the frugality of Yu of Xia, and drawn together the classical learning of Yin and Zhou. I could do nothing but sing your praise—what more is left for me to say?

sentences.zh: 惟未舉清遠有禮之臣，以敦風節；

translations.literal: Only you have not yet promoted ministers who are pure, far-reaching, and observant of propriety, in order to thicken custom and integrity;
translations.idiomatic: Only this remains: you have not yet raised up ministers who combine purity, depth, and ritual decorum, men who could give backbone to public conduct;

sentences.zh: 未退虛鄙，以懲不恪，臣是以猶敢有言。

translations.literal: nor have you dismissed the empty and base to punish lack of reverence—therefore your subject for this reason still dares to have words.
translations.idiomatic: nor have you cleared away the hollow and the mean to punish slackness—and for that reason I still presume to speak.

sentences.zh: 」詔報曰：「舉清遠有禮之臣者，此尤今之要也。

translations.literal: " The edict replied: "To promote ministers who are pure, far-reaching, and observant of propriety—this is especially what is essential today."
translations.idiomatic: " The court answered with an edict: "Promoting men who are pure, serious, and observant of ritual is precisely what the age most urgently needs."

sentences.zh: 」乃使玄草詔進之。

translations.literal: " Then he had Xuan draft an edict to advance them.
translations.idiomatic: " He thereupon told Fu Xuan to draft an edict carrying the policy forward.

sentences.zh: 玄復上疏曰：

translations.literal: Xuan again submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan submitted another memorial:

sentences.zh: 書奏，帝下詔曰：「二常侍懇懇於所論，可謂乃心欲佐益時事者也。

translations.literal: When the document was presented, the emperor issued an edict saying: "The two regular attendants have been earnest in what they discussed; they may be called to give their hearts wishing to aid and benefit the affairs of the times."
translations.idiomatic: When the memorial reached him, the emperor issued an edict: "The two attendant cavaliers have argued their case with real conviction; they clearly mean to put their hearts into improving the business of government."

sentences.zh: 而主者率以常制裁之，豈得不使發憤耶！

translations.literal: Yet those in charge routinely dispose of it by regular procedures—how could that not make one resent it in anger!
translations.idiomatic: Yet the bureaus keep folding everything back into routine paperwork—no wonder honest men boil with frustration!

sentences.zh: 二常侍所論，或舉其大較而未備其條目，亦可便令作之，然後主者八坐廣共研精。

translations.literal: What the two regular attendants debated perhaps raises its general drift but does not complete each item; you may also conveniently have them compose it, after which the presiding officials and the eight seats should together broadly refine it.
translations.idiomatic: What the two cavaliers propose may state the broad outline without filling in every clause; let them draft a fuller version, then have the responsible ministers and the eight senior seats work through the details together.

sentences.zh: 凡關言於人主，人臣之所至難。

translations.literal: Generally, matters that concern speaking to the human ruler are what subjects find hardest.
translations.idiomatic: Speaking truth to the sovereign is the hardest thing a subject can do.

sentences.zh: 而人主若不能虛心聽納，自古忠臣直士之所慷慨，至使杜口結舌。

translations.literal: If the human ruler cannot listen and accept with an empty mind, from antiquity loyal ministers and straight men have for this reason been stirred to passion, to the point of sealing their mouths and binding their tongues.
translations.idiomatic: If the ruler will not listen with an open mind, loyal ministers have always grown desperate and ended by holding their tongues altogether.

sentences.zh: 每念於此，未嘗不歎息也。

translations.literal: Whenever I think of this, I have never failed to sigh.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I think of it, I cannot help but sigh.

sentences.zh: 故前詔敢有直言，勿有所距，庶幾得以發懞補過，獲保高位。

translations.literal: Therefore in the earlier edict I dared to have straight speech and nothing refused, hoping thereby to be able to air ignorance and mend faults, and obtain preservation of high rank.
translations.idiomatic: That is why my earlier edict invited blunt speech and forbade anyone to block it—I hoped ignorance might be aired, faults corrected, and high office kept secure.

sentences.zh: 苟言有偏善，情在忠益，雖文辭有謬誤，言語有失得，皆當曠然恕之。

translations.literal: If in what is said there is partial good, and the intent is in loyalty and benefit—even if diction has errors and speech has misses and gains—all should be broadly and clearly forgiven.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever a remark contains even a partial good point and the speaker means loyalty and the public good, I should overlook clumsy wording or slips of the tongue and forgive him outright.

sentences.zh: 古人猶不拒誹謗，況皆善意在可採錄乎！

translations.literal: The ancients still did not refuse slander; how much more when all are good intentions and there is something that can be selected and recorded!
translations.idiomatic: The ancients did not even refuse bitter criticism; how much less should I reject advice offered in good faith and worth taking down!

sentences.zh: 近者孔晁、綦毋龢皆案以輕慢之罪，所以皆原，欲使四海知區區之朝無諱言之忌也。

translations.literal: Recently Kong Chao and Qi Wu He were both sentenced on the crime of slight disrespect; the reason they were all pardoned was to desire to let the four seas know that this humble court has no taboo against speaking one's mind.
translations.idiomatic: Not long ago Kong Chao and Qi Wu He were charged with disrespect; I pardoned them both so that the empire would see this court has no fear of plain speaking.

sentences.zh: 」俄遷侍中。

translations.literal: " Soon after he was promoted to palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: " Soon afterward Fu Xuan was promoted to palace attendant.

sentences.zh: 初，玄進皇甫陶，及入而抵，玄以事與陶爭，言喧嘩，為有司所奏，二人竟坐免官。

translations.literal: At first Xuan had recommended Huangfu Tao, but when [Tao] entered they clashed; Xuan over affairs quarrelled with Tao, words were noisy and clamorous, they were reported by the authorities, and in the end both sat and were dismissed from office.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, Fu Xuan had recommended Huangfu Tao, but once Tao took office the two men fell out; they quarreled loudly over policy until the authorities impeached them, and both were stripped of their posts.

sentences.zh: ，以為御史中丞。

translations.literal: The clause reads only ', and he was made metropolitan censor,' with the preceding subject lost in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: He was appointed metropolitan censor, though the preceding words are lost in the received text.

sentences.zh: 時頗有水旱之災，玄復上疏曰：

translations.literal: At that time there were rather frequent flood and drought disasters; Xuan again submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: Floods and droughts were then plaguing the realm, and Fu Xuan again addressed a memorial to the throne:

sentences.zh: 詔曰：「得所陳便宜，言農事得失及水官興廢，又安邊禦胡政事寬猛之宜，申省周備，一二具之，此誠為國大本，當今急務也。

translations.literal: An edict said: "Having received the conveniences you set forth—speaking of farming affairs' gains and losses and water offices' rise and fall, also the fit of lenience and severity in governing the frontiers and repelling the Hu—laid out clearly and completely item by item—this is truly the great root of the state and the urgent task of the present."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor replied by edict: "Your practical proposals on the successes and failures of agriculture, on which water offices to keep or abolish, and on how to balance severity and leniency in securing the frontier against the Hu are set out with admirable clarity. These are indeed fundamental matters for the state and pressing tasks for today."

sentences.zh: 如所論皆善，深知乃心，廣思諸宜，動靜以聞也。」

translations.literal: If as you discuss all is good, I know deeply what is in your heart; think broadly on every suitable measure, and by movement and stillness report it."
translations.idiomatic: If everything you argue is sound, know that I understand your intent; think through every suitable measure and keep me informed as circumstances change."

sentences.zh: 五年，遷太僕。

translations.literal: In the fifth year, he was promoted to grand coachman.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth year of the reign he was promoted to grand coachman.

sentences.zh: 時比年不登，羌胡擾邊，詔公卿會議。

translations.literal: At that time year after year the harvests did not ripen, the Qiang and Hu disturbed the borders, and an edict ordered dukes and ministers to meet in council.
translations.idiomatic: Harvests had failed year after year, Qiang and Hu raiders harried the frontier, and the court ordered the high ministers to convene for deliberation.

sentences.zh: 玄應對所問，陳事切直，雖不盡施行，而常見優容。

translations.literal: In answering what was asked Xuan stated matters incisively and directly; though not everything was fully put into practice, he was often shown favor and tolerance.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan answered every question put to him with blunt, searching analysis; not all of his advice was adopted, but the throne regularly treated him with patience and favor.

sentences.zh: 轉司隸校尉。

translations.literal: He was transferred to colonel director of retainers.
translations.idiomatic: He was then transferred to the post of colonel director of retainers.

sentences.zh: 獻皇后崩于弘訓宮，設喪位。

translations.literal: Empress Xian died in the Hongxun Palace, and mourning stations were set up.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Xian died in Hongxun Palace, and mourning stations were arranged for the rites.

sentences.zh: 舊制，司隸於端門外坐，在諸卿上，絕席。

translations.literal: By old regulation the colonel director of retainers sat outside the Duan Gate, above the various ministers, on a separate mat.
translations.idiomatic: By established precedent the colonel director of retainers took his seat outside the Duan Gate above the other ministers, on a separate mat that marked his precedence.

sentences.zh: 其入殿，按本品秩在諸卿下，以次坐，不絕席。

translations.literal: When entering the hall, according to his original grade and rank he was below the various ministers, sitting in order, not on a separate mat.
translations.idiomatic: When he entered the main hall, his nominal rank placed him below the ministers in order of seating, without the privilege of a separate mat.

sentences.zh: 而謁者以弘訓宮為殿內，制玄位在卿下。

translations.literal: But the usher took the Hongxun Palace as being inside the hall and regulated Xuan's seat to be below the ministers.
translations.idiomatic: The ushers treated Hongxun Palace as part of the inner palace and therefore assigned Fu Xuan a place below the ministers.

sentences.zh: 玄恚怒，厲聲色而責謁者。

translations.literal: Xuan was angry and furious, and in severe voice and countenance rebuked the usher.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xuan flared with rage and berated the ushers in a harsh voice.

sentences.zh: 謁者妄稱尚書所處，玄對百僚而罵尚書以下。

translations.literal: The usher falsely claimed it was where the secretariat had placed him; Xuan in front of the hundred officials berated the secretariat downward.
translations.idiomatic: The ushers falsely claimed the secretariat had fixed the seating; Fu Xuan then reviled the secretariat and everyone below it in full view of the court.

sentences.zh: 御史中丞庾純奏玄不敬，玄又自表不以實，坐免官。

translations.literal: Metropolitan censor Yu Chun memorialized that Xuan had been disrespectful; Xuan also self-reported not according to truth; by verdict he was dismissed from office.
translations.idiomatic: Metropolitan censor Yu Chun impeached him for disrespect; Fu Xuan's own written defense was deemed untruthful, and he was dismissed from office.

sentences.zh: 然玄天性峻急，不能有所容；

translations.literal: Yet Xuan by nature was steep and hasty and could accommodate nothing.
translations.idiomatic: By nature Fu Xuan was harsh and impatient, and he made allowance for no one.

sentences.zh: 每有奏劾，或值日暮，捧白簡，整簪帶，竦踴不寐，坐而待旦。

translations.literal: Whenever he had a memorial of impeachment, sometimes it happened to be dusk; he would grasp the white tablet, straighten hairpin and belt, stand bolt upright and leap, not sleep, and sit waiting for dawn.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever he prepared an impeachment, even if night was falling, he would take up his white indictment tablet, straighten cap and sash, sit bolt upright without sleep, and wait for dawn.

sentences.zh: 於是貴遊懾伏，臺閣生風。

translations.literal: Thereupon the noble and wandering were awed into submission, and the terraces and pavilions produced wind.
translations.idiomatic: The great families trembled into submission, and a new austerity swept through the bureaus.

sentences.zh: 尋卒于家，時年六十二，諡曰剛。

translations.literal: Soon he died at home; at the time his age was sixty-two; his posthumous title was called Gang.
translations.idiomatic: He died at home not long afterward, aged sixty-two, with the posthumous name Gang, "the unyielding."

sentences.zh: 玄少時避難於河內，專心誦學，後雖顯貴，而著述不廢。

translations.literal: In youth Xuan took refuge from troubles in Henei and devoted his mind to reciting and learning; later although he was eminent and noble, yet writing was not abandoned.
translations.idiomatic: In his youth he had fled trouble to Henei and given himself entirely to study; even after he rose to high rank he never set scholarship aside.

sentences.zh: 撰論經國九流及三史故事，評斷得失，各為區例，名為《傅子》，為內、外、中篇，凡有四部、六錄，合百四十首，數十萬言，並文集百餘卷行於世。

translations.literal: He composed discourses on ordering the state and the nine currents and on stories from the three histories, judging gains and losses, each establishing categories and examples, named the *Collected Master Fu*—inner, outer, and middle sections—in all four parts, six registers, totaling 140 pieces, several hundred thousand graphs, together with a literary collection of over a hundred fascicles that circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote treatises on statecraft and the nine schools of thought, drew lessons from the three histories, weighed right and wrong, and arranged his conclusions by topic in a work called the *Fu zi*, divided into inner, outer, and middle books—four sections, six registers, one hundred forty chapters and several hundred thousand characters—together with a literary collection of more than a hundred fascicles that circulated widely.

sentences.zh: 玄初作內篇成，子咸以示司空王沈。

translations.literal: When Xuan first finished composing the inner chapters, his son Xian showed them to Minister of Works Wang Chen.
translations.idiomatic: When Fu Xuan had finished the first part of the inner books, his son Fu Xian showed the manuscript to Wang Chen, the minister of works.

sentences.zh: 沈與玄書曰：「省足下所著書，言富理濟，經綸政體，存重儒教，足以塞楊、墨之流遁，齊孫、孟于往代。

translations.literal: Chen wrote to Xuan saying: "I have examined what your feet have written; the words are rich and the principles sustain; in ordering the threads of government it preserves and values Confucian teaching—enough to block the Yang and Mo schools' flow and evasion, and align Sun and Mencius with past ages."
translations.idiomatic: Wang Chen wrote to Fu Xuan: "I have read what you have written; the language is ample and the argument sound. In ordering the body politic you give due weight to Confucian teaching—enough to shut the door on the evasions of Yang Zhu and Mozi and to set Sunzi and Mencius on a par with the best of antiquity."

sentences.zh: 每開卷，未嘗不歎息也。

translations.literal: Whenever I open a scroll, I have never failed to sigh.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I open the manuscript I find myself sighing in admiration.

sentences.zh: 『不見賈生，自以過之，乃今不及』，信矣！」

translations.literal: 'Not having seen Master Jia, I thought I surpassed him; now I am not his equal'—how true!"
translations.idiomatic: As the saying goes, 'Before I met Jia Yi I thought I surpassed him; now I see I do not measure up'—how true that is!"

sentences.zh: 其後追封清泉侯。

translations.literal: Afterwards he was posthumously enfeoffed as marquis of Qingquan.
translations.idiomatic: He was later given the posthumous title of marquis of Qingquan.

sentences.zh: 子咸嗣。

translations.literal: His son Xian inherited.
translations.idiomatic: His son Fu Xian inherited the title.

translations.literal: Equals sign.
translations.idiomatic: The source text here consists only of a stray equals mark, probably a section divider or typographical artifact.

sentences.zh: 子咸

translations.literal: Son Xian.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian

sentences.zh: =咸字長虞，剛簡有大節。

translations.literal: Xian, style name Changyu, was stern and simple and had great integrity.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian, courtesy name Changyu, was austere and plain-spoken and showed unbending integrity in great matters.

sentences.zh: 風格峻整，識性明悟，疾惡如仇，推賢樂善，常慕季文子、仲山甫之志。

translations.literal: His manner and pattern were stern and ordered, his knowledge and nature bright and perceptive; he hated evil as if an enemy, promoted the worthy and delighted in the good, and often admired the aims of Ji Wenzi and Zhong Shanfu.
translations.idiomatic: His bearing was severe and composed, his judgment lucid; he hated wickedness as he would a personal enemy, lifted up the worthy, and delighted in the good, and he modeled himself on the aspirations of Ji Wenzi and Zhong Shanfu of old.

sentences.zh: 好屬文論，雖綺麗不足，而言成規鑒。

translations.literal: He was fond of composing texts and disquisitions; though ornate beauty was insufficient, yet his words formed regulation and mirror.
translations.idiomatic: He loved to write essays and memorials; they lacked ornamental brilliance, but every piece offered clear standards and sober judgment.

sentences.zh: 潁川庾純常歎曰：「長虞之文近乎詩人之作矣！」

translations.literal: Yu Chun of Yingchuan often sighed saying: "Changyu's texts are close to the work of the poets!"
translations.idiomatic: Yu Chun of Yingchuan used to exclaim, "Changyu's prose is almost what we call poetry!"

sentences.zh: 咸甯初，襲父爵，拜太子洗馬，累遷尚書右丞。

translations.literal: In the early Xianning era he inherited his father's noble rank, was appointed erudite of the heir apparent, and by stages was promoted to right assistant of the secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Xianning era he inherited his father's noble rank, was appointed tutor to the heir apparent, and rose through several posts to right assistant in the secretariat.

sentences.zh: 出為冀州刺史，繼母杜氏不肯隨咸之官，自表解職。

translations.literal: He went out to be inspector of Ji Province; his stepmother Lady Du was unwilling to follow Xian to his post, so he personally memorialized requesting release from duty.
translations.idiomatic: When he was sent out as inspector of Ji, his stepmother, Lady Du, refused to accompany him to his post, so he asked to resign.

sentences.zh: 三旬之間，遷司徒左長史。

translations.literal: Within thirty days he was promoted to senior clerk in the left of the minister of education.
translations.idiomatic: Within thirty days he was promoted to senior clerk on the left of the minister of education.

sentences.zh: 時帝留心政事，詔訪朝臣政之損益。

translations.literal: At that time the emperor applied his mind to government affairs; an edict inquired of court ministers about harm and benefit in administration.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor was then intent on government and issued an edict asking the ministers what in current policy helped or harmed the realm.

sentences.zh: 咸上言曰：「陛下處至尊之位，而修布衣之事，親覽萬機，勞心日昃。

translations.literal: Xian submitted words saying: "Your Majesty occupies the supremely honored position, yet cultivates common-cloth affairs, personally inspects ten thousand threads, and toils in mind until the sun slants.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian began by saying that although Your Majesty sits on the highest throne, you take on a commoner's workload, personally handling every thread of government from dawn until the sun is low in the west.

sentences.zh: 在昔帝王，躬自菲薄，以利天下，未有逾陛下也。

translations.literal: Among emperors and kings of the past who personally practiced meagerness to benefit all under Heaven, none has exceeded Your Majesty.
translations.idiomatic: Among the emperors of old who wore austerity on their own backs for the good of the realm, none has outdone you.

sentences.zh: 然泰始開元以暨於今，十有五年矣。

translations.literal: Yet from the opening of Taishi down to the present, there are already fifteen years.
translations.idiomatic: Yet fifteen years have passed since the Taishi era began.

sentences.zh: 而軍國未豐，百姓不贍，一歲不登便有菜色者，誠由官眾事殷，復除猥濫，蠶食者多而親農者少也。

translations.literal: Yet the army and state are not abundant, the hundred surnames are not sufficient; if for one year the harvest does not ascend then there are those with vegetable color—truly it is because officials are many and affairs are pressing, exemptions are excessive and loose, those who nibble away are many while those who personally farm are few.
translations.idiomatic: The army and the treasury are still poor, the people still lack reserves: a single bad harvest puts hunger in their faces. The reason is plain—too many officials, too many tasks, tax relief handed out indiscriminately, endless petty predators on the countryside, and too few hands actually at the plow.

sentences.zh: 臣以頑疏，謬忝近職，每見聖詔以百姓饑饉為慮，無能雲補，伏用慚恧，敢不自竭，以對天問。

translations.literal: Your subject, by dullness and roughness, wrongly is honored with a nearby post; whenever I see the sagely edict take the hundred surnames' hunger and famine as anxiety, unable to add even a cloud's worth of help, I prostrate in shame—yet I dare not fail to exhaust myself in answering Heaven's question.
translations.idiomatic: I am a dull man unworthy of a place near the throne, yet whenever I read your edicts' anguish over the people's hunger I burn with shame that I have offered no help worth mentioning; I can only pour out what little I know in answer to your question.

sentences.zh: 舊都督有四，今並監軍，乃盈於十。

translations.literal: Formerly area commanders were four; now together with army supervisors they exceed ten.
translations.idiomatic: There used to be four regional commanders; with army supervisors added in, the number is now well over ten.

sentences.zh: 夏禹敷土，分為九州，今之刺史，幾向一倍。

translations.literal: Great Yu spread the soil and divided it into nine provinces; today's regional inspectors approach nearly double.
translations.idiomatic: Great Yu mapped the realm into nine provinces; we now maintain nearly twice as many provincial inspectors.

sentences.zh: 戶口比漢十分之一，而置郡縣更多。

translations.literal: Households and mouths are one-tenth compared to the Han, yet established commanderies and counties are more numerous.
translations.idiomatic: Registered households are barely a tenth of what they were under the Han, yet we have more commanderies and counties than ever.

sentences.zh: 空校牙門，無益宿衛，而虛立軍府，動有百數。

translations.literal: Empty posts at headquarters gates bring no benefit to night guard, yet hollowly army offices are established—often reaching a hundred-odd.
translations.idiomatic: Idle posts clutter headquarters gates without strengthening the night watch, while empty army bureaus are opened by the hundred.

sentences.zh: 五等諸侯，復坐置官屬。

translations.literal: The nobles of the five ranks again sit while appointing official subordinates.
translations.idiomatic: The nobles of the five ranks sit in office while piling up personal staffs.

sentences.zh: 諸所寵給，皆生於百姓。

translations.literal: All that is lavishly granted is born from the hundred surnames.
translations.idiomatic: Every one of those salaries is wrung from the common people.

sentences.zh: 一夫不農，有受其饑，今之不農，不可勝計。

translations.literal: If one man does not farm, there is one who receives his hunger; of today's not farming, the number cannot be counted.
translations.idiomatic: If one man leaves the plow, someone goes hungry; today the number of men not farming is beyond counting.

sentences.zh: 縱使五稼普收，僅足相接；

translations.literal: Even if the five grains were universally harvested, it would barely be enough to connect;
translations.idiomatic: Even if every crop ripened well, the harvest would barely meet consumption;

sentences.zh: 暫有災患，便不繼贍。

translations.literal: Briefly if there is disaster or hardship, then it does not continue to provision.
translations.idiomatic: the slightest disaster breaks the chain of supply.

sentences.zh: 以為當今之急，先並官省事，靜事息役，上下用心，惟農是務也。」

translations.literal: Your subject holds that the urgency of the present is first to merge offices and cut affairs, still affairs and rest corvée, above and below apply their minds, and farming alone is the task.
translations.idiomatic: I therefore believe the first task is to merge offices, cut redundant business, quiet lawsuits, and lighten corvée so that high and low alike bend their efforts to farming alone.

sentences.zh: 咸在位多所執正。

translations.literal: Xian in office often upheld what was correct in many things.
translations.idiomatic: In office Fu Xian repeatedly stood his ground on points of principle.

sentences.zh: 豫州大中正夏侯駿上言，魯國小中正、司空司馬孔毓，四移病所，不能接賓，求以尚書郎曹馥代毓，旬日復上毓為中正。

translations.literal: The grand rectifier of Yu Province, Xiahou Jun, submitted a statement that Kong Yu, minor rectifier of Lu and a major to the minister of works, had shifted his sick residence four times and could not receive guests, requesting to replace Yu with Cao Fu, gentleman of the secretariat; after ten days he again submitted Yu as rectifier.
translations.idiomatic: Xiahou Jun, the grand rectifier for Yu province, reported that Kong Yu—minor rectifier for Lu and a staff major under the minister of works—had changed his sick-leave residence four times and could not receive visitors; he asked that Cao Fu, a gentleman of the secretariat, replace Kong Yu, then ten days later submitted Kong Yu's name again for the rectifier's post.

sentences.zh: 司徒三卻，駿故據正。

translations.literal: The minister of education thrice rejected; Jun therefore held to rectitude.
translations.idiomatic: The minister of education rejected the nomination three times, but Xiahou Jun stubbornly insisted he was right.

sentences.zh: 咸以駿與奪惟意，乃奏免駿大中正。

translations.literal: Xian, because Jun's granting and taking away followed whim, then memorialized to dismiss Jun as grand rectifier.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian held that Xiahou Jun was making appointments and dismissals on whim, and memorialized to remove him as grand rectifier.

sentences.zh: 司徒魏舒，駿之姻屬，屢卻不署，咸據正甚苦。

translations.literal: Minister of Education Wei Shu, Jun's marriage-relative, repeatedly rejected and would not sign; Xian held to rectitude with great bitterness.
translations.idiomatic: The minister of education, Wei Shu—related to Xiahou Jun by marriage—repeatedly refused to countersign; Fu Xian pressed his case with bitter persistence.

sentences.zh: 舒終不從，咸遂獨上。

translations.literal: Shu in the end did not comply; Xian thereupon submitted alone.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Shu still would not yield, so Fu Xian submitted his memorial alone.

sentences.zh: 舒奏咸激訕不直，詔轉咸為車騎司馬。

translations.literal: Shu memorialized that Xian was provocative and slanderous and not straight; by edict Xian was transferred to be marshal of the chariots and cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Shu then accused Fu Xian of provocation and slander; the court transferred Fu Xian to the post of marshal in the chariots-and-cavalry command.

sentences.zh: 咸以世俗奢侈，又上書曰：「臣以為穀帛難生，而用之不節，無緣不匱。

translations.literal: Xian, because the customs of the age were extravagant, also submitted a memorial saying: "Your subject holds that grain and silk are hard to produce, and if they are used without restraint, there is no cause for them not to be exhausted."
translations.idiomatic: Distressed by the luxury of the age, Fu Xian sent up another memorial: "Grain and silk are hard to come by; if we spend them without restraint, they cannot fail to run short."

sentences.zh: 故先王之化天下，食肉衣帛，皆有其制。

translations.literal: Therefore former kings' transforming all under Heaven—eating meat and wearing silk—each had its regulation.
translations.idiomatic: The kings of old who civilized the realm laid down clear rules even for such things as eating meat and wearing silk."

sentences.zh: 竊謂奢侈之費，甚於天災。

translations.literal: Your subject privately holds that the expense of extravagance exceeds natural disaster.
translations.idiomatic: I would add that the waste of extravagance does more harm than flood or drought."

sentences.zh: 古者堯有茅茨，今之百姓競豐其屋。

translations.literal: In antiquity Yao had thatched huts; the common people of today vie to make their houses lavish.
translations.idiomatic: In Yao’s day the ruler lived under a thatched roof; today ordinary families compete to build ever grander houses.

sentences.zh: 古者臣無玉食，今之賈豎皆厭粱肉。

translations.literal: In antiquity ministers had no jade food; today’s merchant lads all are sated with fine millet and meat.
translations.idiomatic: Once, ministers did not dine off jade vessels; today even petty traders grow weary of the finest grain and meat.

sentences.zh: 古者后妃乃有殊飾，今之婢妾被服綾羅。

translations.literal: In antiquity only empresses and consorts had special ornaments; today’s maids and concubines are clothed in gauze and thin silk.
translations.idiomatic: Ornaments once reserved for queens and consorts now wrap maids and concubines in damask and gauze.

sentences.zh: 古者大夫乃不徒行，今之賤隸乘輕驅肥。

translations.literal: In antiquity only grandees did not walk on foot; today’s base bondsmen ride light carriages and drive fat horses.
translations.idiomatic: Grandees alone once rode rather than walked; today the meanest servants clip along in light carriages behind sleek horses.

sentences.zh: 古者人稠地狹而有儲蓄，由於節也；

translations.literal: In antiquity people were dense and land narrow yet there were stores—this was because of restraint;
translations.idiomatic: When population pressed on narrow land, people still saved—because they lived frugally;

sentences.zh: 今者土廣人稀而患不足，由於奢也。

translations.literal: Today land is wide and people sparse yet we worry about insufficiency—this is because of extravagance.
translations.idiomatic: Now the realm is wide and thinly peopled, yet we fret over want—because we have grown extravagant.

sentences.zh: 欲時之儉，當詰其奢；

translations.literal: To seek frugality for the age, one must investigate its extravagance;
translations.idiomatic: If you want the age to be thrifty, you must call its extravagance to account;

sentences.zh: 奢不見詰，轉相高尚。

translations.literal: If extravagance is not investigated, they turn and esteem one another ever more highly.
translations.idiomatic: if extravagance goes unchallenged, people only egg one another on toward finer taste.

sentences.zh: 昔毛玠為吏部尚書，時無敢好衣美食者。

translations.literal: In the past when Mao Jie was director of the ministry of appointments, for a time none dared love fine clothes or good food.
translations.idiomatic: When Mao Jie headed the ministry of appointments, for a while no one dared flaunt fine dress or rich food.

sentences.zh: 魏武帝歎曰：『孤之法不如毛尚書。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei sighed: “My laws are not the equal of Director Mao.”
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao sighed, “My statutes do not match Director Mao’s standards.”

sentences.zh: 』令使諸部用心，各如毛玠，風俗之移，在不難矣。

translations.literal: If we ordered every department to apply their minds each as Mao Jie did, shifting custom would not be difficult.
translations.idiomatic: If every bureau could apply itself as Mao Jie did, changing the temper of the times would not be hard.

sentences.zh: 」又議移縣獄於郡及二社應立，朝廷從之。

translations.literal: He also debated moving county prisons to the commandery and establishing the two altars of soil and grain; the court accepted.
translations.idiomatic: He also urged moving county jails to the commandery level and founding the paired altars of soil and grain; the court agreed.

sentences.zh: 遷尚書左丞。

translations.literal: He was promoted to left assistant in the secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to left assistant director in the secretariat.

sentences.zh: 惠帝即位，楊駿輔政。

translations.literal: When Emperor Hui mounted the throne, Yang Jun assisted the government.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Hui came to the throne, Yang Jun directed the government as regent.

sentences.zh: 咸言於駿曰：「事與世變，禮隨時宜，諒暗之不行尚矣。

translations.literal: Xian spoke to Jun, saying: “Affairs change with the age; ritual follows what fits the times; that mourning seclusion is not practiced has long been clear.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian said to Yang Jun: “Circumstances change with the times, and ritual must suit the moment; it has been clear for ages that the old palace mourning cannot be kept unchanged.”

sentences.zh: 由世道彌薄，權不可假，故雖斬焉在疚，而躬覽萬機也。

translations.literal: Because the Way of the world grows ever thinner, power cannot be lent away; therefore although one is cutting grief in deep mourning, yet one personally inspects the ten thousand threads of business.”
translations.idiomatic: The moral climate has thinned, and supreme authority cannot be handed off; that is why even a ruler in the deepest mourning still has to take up the myriad affairs of state himself.”

sentences.zh: 逮至漢文，以天下體大，服重難久，遂制既葬而除。

translations.literal: Down to Emperor Wen of Han, because the realm under Heaven was large in scale and heavy mourning could not be prolonged long, thereupon the rule was to remove mourning garments once burial was complete.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen of Han, seeing the realm too vast for prolonged heavy mourning, decreed that mourning dress end with the burial.

sentences.zh: 世祖武皇帝雖大孝蒸蒸，亦從時釋服，制心喪三年，至於萬機之事，則有不遑。

translations.literal: Our founding emperor Emperor Wu, though his filial devotion was abundant, also followed the times in laying aside mourning garments, setting heart-mourning for three years; as for the ten thousand threads of business, then there was no leisure.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu, our dynastic founder, was deeply filial, yet he too laid aside formal mourning when the times required it, keeping a three-year grief in his heart while knowing he could not neglect the myriad tasks of rule.

sentences.zh: 今聖上欲委政於公，諒暗自居，此雖謙讓之心，而天下未以為善。

translations.literal: Now the sagely sovereign wishes to entrust government to your lordship and dwell in mourning seclusion himself—this, although a mind of yielding, is not what all under Heaven takes for good.
translations.idiomatic: The reigning emperor wishes to leave government in your hands while he withdraws in mourning; that may show modest intent, but the empire does not read it as wise.

sentences.zh: 天下未以為善者，以億兆顒顒，戴仰宸極，聽於冢宰，懼天光有蔽。

translations.literal: The reason all under Heaven does not take it for good is that the millions lift their heads, looking up to the pole star; hearing that the grand steward alone decides, they fear the heavenly light may be blocked.
translations.idiomatic: People look up to the throne alone; if they hear that only the chief minister decides policy, they fear the sovereign’s light will be hidden.

sentences.zh: 人心既已若此，而明公處之固未為易也。

translations.literal: Human hearts are already like this, yet your lordship’s handling of it is surely not easy.
translations.idiomatic: Hearts are already uneasy; for you, sir, the position cannot be an easy one.

sentences.zh: 竊謂山陵之事既畢，明公當思隆替之宜。

translations.literal: Your subject privately holds that once matters on the hills and tombs are finished, your lordship ought to weigh what suits flourishing or decline.
translations.idiomatic: Once the imperial burial is over, you must weigh what will strengthen the state and what will weaken it.

sentences.zh: 周公聖人，猶不免謗。

translations.literal: The Duke of Zhou was a sage, yet even he could not escape slander.
translations.idiomatic: Even the Duke of Zhou, a sage, could not escape slander.

sentences.zh: 以此推之，周公之任既未易而處，況聖上春秋非成王之年乎！

translations.literal: From this one infers: the Duke of Zhou’s burden was already not easy to bear—how much more when the sagely sovereign’s years do not match King Cheng’s!
translations.idiomatic: If the Duke of Zhou’s burden was hard to bear, how much harder when our emperor is not a child like King Cheng of old!

sentences.zh: 得意忘言，言未易盡。

translations.literal: When the meaning is grasped, words are forgotten; words are not easy to exhaust.
translations.idiomatic: When the point is taken, words may cease; yet words can never say everything.

sentences.zh: 苟明公有以察其悾款，言豈在多。

translations.literal: If your lordship can see the sincerity in my earnest dullness, words need not be many.
translations.idiomatic: If you can see the earnest loyalty behind my bluntness, I need not say more.

sentences.zh: 」時司隸荀愷從兄喪，自表赴哀，詔聽之而未下，愷乃造駿。

translations.literal: At that time the colonel director of retainers Xun Kai, on a cousin’s death, personally memorialized to go to mourning; an edict had approved it but not yet been issued, yet Kai went to Jun’s place.
translations.idiomatic: Meanwhile Xun Kai, the colonel director of retainers, had petitioned to mourn a deceased cousin; the throne had granted leave but the edict had not yet been issued when Kai went to Yang Jun’s house.

sentences.zh: 咸因奏曰：「死喪之戚，兄弟孔懷。

translations.literal: Xian thereupon memorialized: “The grief of death: brothers greatly cherish one another.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian seized on this and memorialized: “The grief of death strikes brothers most keenly.”

sentences.zh: 同堂亡隕，方在信宿，聖恩矜憫，聽使臨喪。

translations.literal: A hall-mate has died and fallen; we are still within two nights; the sagely grace pities and allows attendance at mourning.”
translations.idiomatic: A cousin has just died; barely two nights have passed. The court in its mercy would let him attend the rites.”

sentences.zh: 詔未下而便以行造，急諂媚之敬，無友于之情。

translations.literal: The edict had not been issued yet he used motion to go pay visit—hasty flattery’s reverence, no fraternal feeling toward friends.
translations.idiomatic: To hurry to a private visit before the edict appears is eager flattery, not the affection due between brothers.

sentences.zh: 宜加顯貶，以隆風教。

translations.literal: He ought plainly to be demoted to thicken customs and teaching.”
translations.idiomatic: He should be publicly demoted to uphold public morals.”

sentences.zh: 」帝以駿管朝政，有詔不問，駿甚憚之。

translations.literal: The emperor, because Jun controlled court government, issued an edict not to pursue the matter; Jun greatly feared him.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor, because Yang Jun ran the government, ordered the charge dropped; Jun nonetheless came to fear Fu Xian deeply.

sentences.zh: 咸復與駿箋諷切之，駿意稍折，漸以不平。

translations.literal: Xian again wrote Jun a letter exhorting him incisively; Jun’s intent bent slightly but gradually turned resentful.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian wrote again to needle Yang Jun; Jun yielded a little on the surface but grew quietly resentful.

sentences.zh: 由是欲出為京兆、弘農太守，駿甥李斌說駿，不宜斥出正人，乃止。

translations.literal: Thereupon [Jun] wished to send [Xian] out as governor of Jingzhao or Hongnong; Jun’s nephew Li Bin persuaded Jun that one should not expel an upright man, and so it stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Jun then planned to send Fu Xian out as governor of Jingzhao or Hongnong, but Li Bin, Jun’s nephew, argued that an upright man should not be banished from the capital, and Jun dropped the idea.

sentences.zh: 駿弟濟素與咸善，與咸書曰：「江海之流混混，故能成其深廣也。

translations.literal: Jun’s younger brother Ji had always been on good terms with Xian; he wrote to Xian: “River and sea currents are turbid and vast, therefore they can achieve depth and breadth.”
translations.idiomatic: Yang Ji, Jun’s younger brother, who was friendly with Fu Xian, wrote: “Rivers and seas run broad and muddy, and that is how they grow deep and wide.”

sentences.zh: 天下大器，非可稍了，而相觀每事欲了。

translations.literal: The great vessel of all under Heaven cannot be grasped in little bits; yet you inspect everything wishing to get it all done.
translations.idiomatic: The empire is no trifle to be ticked off in pieces, yet you try to finish every matter at a glance.

sentences.zh: 生子癡，了官事，官事未易了也。

translations.literal: Bearing sons is foolish; finishing official matters—official matters are not easy to finish.
translations.idiomatic: The proverb runs, “Raise a dull son, leave him office work”—office work is never really finished.

sentences.zh: 了事正作癡，復為快耳！

translations.literal: Finishing affairs is precisely making foolishness, yet we call it sharp!
translations.idiomatic: To “finish” business is to play the fool, yet people call that clever!

sentences.zh: 左丞總司天臺，維正八坐，此未易居。

translations.literal: The left assistant oversees the celestial terrace and aligns the eight seats—this is not an easy place to stand.
translations.idiomatic: The left assistant steers the high ministries and keeps the eight senior seats in line—that is no easy seat.

sentences.zh: 以君盡性而處未易居之任，益不易也。

translations.literal: That you, with full nature, occupy a place not easy to stand—that is even less easy.
translations.idiomatic: For a man of your uncompromising nature to hold such a post is harder still.

sentences.zh: 想慮破頭，故具有白。

translations.literal: My thoughts worry until they break my head; therefore I write this in full.
translations.idiomatic: I worry until my head aches, so I spell it all out here.

sentences.zh: 」咸答曰：「衛公-{云}-酒色之殺人，此甚於作直。

translations.literal: Xian replied: “Lord Wei says wine and sex kill people—this is worse than acting straight.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian answered: “Lord Wei says wine and lust kill more surely than blunt honesty.”

sentences.zh: 坐酒色死，人不為悔。

translations.literal: Dying through wine and sex, people do not regret it.
translations.idiomatic: Men die of drink and lust without a twinge of regret.

sentences.zh: 逆畏以直致禍，此由心不直正，欲以苟且為明哲耳！

translations.literal: Contrariwise fearing that straightness brings disaster—that is because the heart is not straight and upright, wishing to take evasive compromise as wise clarity!
translations.idiomatic: To shun disaster by silence shows a heart that is not straight—it is cowardice dressed up as wisdom.

sentences.zh: 自古以直致禍者，當自矯枉過直，或不忠允，欲以亢厲為聲，故致忿耳。

translations.literal: From antiquity those who brought disaster on themselves by straightness were either bending the straight too far, or not being loyal and sincere, wishing to borrow harshness for reputation, therefore incurring resentment.
translations.idiomatic: Those who court ruin by bluntness usually overcorrect, or lack true loyalty, or play the martyr for fame—and so they earn resentment.

sentences.zh: 安有空空為忠益，而當見疾乎！

translations.literal: How could blandly being loyal and beneficial then meet with jealousy!
translations.idiomatic: Would plain loyalty for the public good alone earn hatred?

sentences.zh: 」居無何，駿誅。

translations.literal: Before long, Jun was executed.
translations.idiomatic: Soon afterward Yang Jun was executed.

sentences.zh: 咸轉為太子中庶子，遷御史中丞。

translations.literal: Xian was transferred to palace subordinate to the heir apparent, then promoted metropolitan censor.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian was moved to palace attendant to the heir apparent, then promoted to metropolitan censor.

sentences.zh: 時太宰、汝南王亮輔政，咸致書曰：

translations.literal: When the grand preceptor, the king of Runan, Liang directed the government, Xian sent a letter saying:
translations.idiomatic: When the grand preceptor, the king of Runan, Sima Liang, directed policy, Fu Xian wrote to him:

sentences.zh: 咸復以亮輔政專權，又諫曰：「楊駿有震主之威，委任親戚，此天下所以喧嘩。

translations.literal: Xian again, because Liang directed the government and monopolized power, remonstrated: “Yang Jun had awe that shook the ruler, delegating trust to kinsmen—that is why all under Heaven clamored.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian, seeing that Sima Liang monopolized power as regent, remonstrated again: “Yang Jun’s authority overshadowed the throne and he packed office with kin—that is why the realm erupted in protest.”

sentences.zh: 今之處重，宜反此失。

translations.literal: Those who now stand in weight ought to reverse this fault.
translations.idiomatic: Men who hold great power now should undo that mistake.

sentences.zh: 謂宜靜默頤神，有大得失，乃維持之；

translations.literal: I say one ought to keep still, nurture spirit, and only for great gains or losses then uphold them;
translations.idiomatic: You should stay quiet, husband your strength, and intervene only on great issues of right and wrong;

sentences.zh: 自非大事，一皆抑遣。

translations.literal: Whatever is not a great matter should altogether be checked and sent back.
translations.idiomatic: everything short of that should be checked and turned aside.

sentences.zh: 比四造詣，及經過尊門，冠蓋車馬，填塞街衢，此之翕習，既宜弭息。

translations.literal: Recently I have called on you four times, and passing your honored gate, caps and covers, carriages and horses fill and block the streets—this swelling bustle ought at once to be quelled.
translations.idiomatic: Four times lately I have called on you, and each time your gate was choked with carriages and riders; this ostentatious traffic ought to stop.

sentences.zh: 又夏侯長容奉使為先帝請命，祈禱無感，先帝崩背，宜自咎責，而自求請命之勞，而公以為少府。

translations.literal: Further, Xiahou Changrong went on mission to seek life for the late emperor; the prayers were without response; when the late emperor passed away, he ought to have blamed himself, yet he seeks credit for the toil of requesting life—yet your lordship made him minister of the household.
translations.idiomatic: Moreover Xiahou Changrong was sent to pray for the late emperor’s life; the prayers failed; when the emperor died he should have blamed himself, yet he boasted of his mission’s hardship, and you, sir, made him minister of the household.

sentences.zh: 私竊之論，雲長容則公之姻，故至於此。

translations.literal: Private gossip says that Changrong is your lordship’s in-law, and therefore it came to this.
translations.idiomatic: Whispered opinion says Changrong is your kinsman by marriage, which explains the appointment.

sentences.zh: 一犬吠形，群犬吠聲，懼於群吠，遂至叵聽也。

translations.literal: One dog barks at a shape, the pack barks at the sound; fearing the pack’s barking, it becomes unbearable to listen.
translations.idiomatic: One dog barks at a shadow and the pack joins in; fear that chorus and rumor becomes unbearable.

sentences.zh: 咸之為人，不能面從而有後言。

translations.literal: As for Xian’s person, he cannot consent to people’s faces yet later speak otherwise.
translations.idiomatic: I am not the sort to nod assent to your face and murmur behind your back.

sentences.zh: 嘗觸楊駿，幾為身禍；

translations.literal: I once offended Yang Jun and nearly brought bodily disaster on myself;
translations.idiomatic: I once crossed Yang Jun and nearly lost my life;

sentences.zh: 況于殿下，而當有惜！

translations.literal: how much more toward Your Highness—yet should there be reluctance!
translations.idiomatic: how much less would I hold back with you, Your Highness!

sentences.zh: 往從駕，殿下見語：『卿不識韓非逆鱗之言耶，而欻摩天子逆鱗！

translations.literal: Formerly, following the imperial carriage, Your Highness said to me: “Do you not know Han Fei’s words on contrary scales—yet you hastily rub the Son of Heaven’s contrary scales!”
translations.idiomatic: Once, when I attended you on an outing, you said, “Have you not read Han Fei on the ruler’s ‘reverse scales’—yet you keep brushing the emperor’s!”

sentences.zh: 』自知所陳，誠𬱃𬱃觸猛獸之須耳。

translations.literal: I knew that what I stated was truly timidly rubbing the fierce beast’s whiskers.”
translations.idiomatic: I knew my words were timidly tugging the tiger’s whiskers.”

sentences.zh: 所以敢言，庶殿下當識其不勝區區。

translations.literal: The reason I dare to speak is that I hope Your Highness will recognize that I cannot bear but to be utterly sincere.
translations.idiomatic: I speak because I hope you will see how much earnest loyalty compels me.

sentences.zh: 前摩天子逆鱗，欲以盡忠；

translations.literal: Formerly rubbing the Son of Heaven’s contrary scales was in order to exhaust loyalty;
translations.idiomatic: When I pressed the late emperor it was to exhaust my loyalty;

sentences.zh: 今觸猛獸之須，非欲為惡，必將以此見恕。

translations.literal: now touching the fierce beast’s whiskers is not wishing to do evil—it is certain that I will therefore be forgiven.”
translations.idiomatic: now I tug the tiger’s whiskers not from malice but in the trust that you will forgive me.”

sentences.zh: 」亮不納。

translations.literal: Liang did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Liang ignored the advice.

sentences.zh: 長容者，夏侯駿也。

translations.literal: Changrong is Xiahou Jun.
translations.idiomatic: “Changrong” is the style name of Xiahou Jun.

sentences.zh: 會丙寅，詔群僚舉郡縣之職以補內官。

translations.literal: On the bingyin day, an edict ordered the host of officials to recommend commandery and county posts to fill inner offices.
translations.idiomatic: On a bingyin day the court ordered officials to nominate local posts to fill vacancies at the capital.

sentences.zh: 咸復上書曰：

translations.literal: Xian again submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian again addressed a memorial:

sentences.zh: 咸再為本郡中正，遭繼母憂去官。

translations.literal: Xian twice was rectifier for his native commandery; on encountering his stepmother’s bereavement he left office.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian twice served as grand rectifier for his home commandery; he resigned to mourn his stepmother.

sentences.zh: 頃之，起以議郎，長兼司隸校尉。

translations.literal: Before long he was raised up as discussion gentleman, acting concurrently as colonel director of retainers.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as a gentleman consultant and acting colonel director of retainers.

sentences.zh: 咸前後固辭，不聽，敕使者就拜，咸復送還印綬。

translations.literal: Xian repeatedly and firmly declined and was not listened to; the emperor ordered envoys to go invest him, and Xian again sent back the seal and cord.
translations.idiomatic: He declined repeatedly; the court ignored him, sent envoys to invest him in office, and he returned the seal and ribbon again.

sentences.zh: 公車不通，催使攝職。

translations.literal: The public carriage channel was blocked; they pressed him to take up duty.
translations.idiomatic: The petition channel was blocked while the court pressed him to assume the post.

sentences.zh: 咸以身無兄弟，喪祭無主，重自陳乞，乃使於官舍設靈坐。

translations.literal: Xian, because he personally had no brothers and for mourning and sacrifice had no master, heavily stated his plea again; thereupon he was allowed to set up a spirit seat in the official residence.
translations.idiomatic: Because he had no brothers to preside over the rites, he pleaded again at length and was allowed to set up a mourning altar in his official quarters.

sentences.zh: 咸又上表曰：「臣既駑弱，不勝重任。

translations.literal: Xian again submitted a table saying: “Your subject is both blunt and weak, and cannot bear a heavy charge.”
translations.idiomatic: He submitted another memorial: “I am a dull, feeble man unfit for a heavy charge.”

sentences.zh: 加在哀疚，假息日闋，陛下過意，授非所堪。

translations.literal: Added to mourning grief, borrowed breath daily wanes; Your Majesty over-favors me and appoints me to what I cannot sustain.”
translations.idiomatic: Grief has worn me down day by day; Your Majesty overestimates me and gives me duties I cannot sustain.”

sentences.zh: 披露丹款，歸窮上聞，謬詔既往，終然無改。

translations.literal: I have laid bare my crimson sincerity and returned my plea to your ear above; wrongly issued edicts have gone out, yet in the end there is no change.”
translations.idiomatic: I have laid my heart bare and sent my plea to the throne; mistaken edicts went out and nothing was changed.”

sentences.zh: 臣雖不能滅身以全禮教，義無靦然，虛忝隆寵。

translations.literal: Though your subject cannot destroy his person to preserve ritual instruction, in principle there is no way to face it vainly and dishonor excessive favor.”
translations.idiomatic: Though I cannot die to vindicate ritual, I cannot in good conscience accept empty honors.”

sentences.zh: 前受嚴詔，視事之日，私心自誓，隕越為報。

translations.literal: Earlier I received a stern edict; on the day I took up affairs I swore privately that I would dash myself to pieces in repayment.”
translations.idiomatic: When I took office under your stern order I swore I would give my life in return.”

sentences.zh: 以貨賂流行，所宜深絕，切敕都官，以此為先。

translations.literal: Bribery flows and spreads—this ought to be drastically cut off; I urgently charged the capital officials to take this as first priority.”
translations.idiomatic: Bribery was rampant and had to be stopped; I ordered the capital bureaus to strike at it first.”

sentences.zh: 而經彌日月，未有所得。

translations.literal: Yet months have passed and nothing has been obtained.”
translations.idiomatic: Months have passed and nothing has come of it.”

sentences.zh: 斯由陛下有以獎厲，慮於愚戇，將必死系，故自掩檢以避其鋒耳。

translations.literal: This is because Your Majesty has ways to reward and spur them, and they expect that dull fidelity will surely end in death or bonds, therefore they cover and inspect themselves to avoid the edge.”
translations.idiomatic: Your Majesty’s rewards encourage them to think that blunt honesty ends in prison or death, so they hide and lie low to dodge the blow.”

sentences.zh: 在職有日，既無赫然之舉，又不應弦垂翅，人誰復憚？

translations.literal: In office for days, neither having any striking achievement nor like a bowstring snapping a wing—who will again fear?”
translations.idiomatic: I have done nothing dramatic, nor have I broken anyone’s power; why should anyone fear me?”

sentences.zh: 故光祿大夫劉毅為司隸，聲震內外，遠近清肅。

translations.literal: Therefore Grand Counsellor Liu Yi, as colonel director of retainers, his reputation shook within and without, near and far were pure and austere.”
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Yi held this post, his name shook the capital and the regions grew orderly.”

sentences.zh: 非徒毅有王臣匪躬之節，亦由所奏見從，威風得伸也。

translations.literal: It was not only that Yi had the integrity of a royal minister who is not for himself—also because what he memorialized was followed, and his awe-inspiring wind could extend.”
translations.idiomatic: It was not only Liu Yi’s selfless integrity—the throne also backed his memorials, so his authority could bite.”

sentences.zh: 」詔曰：「但當思必應繩中理，威風日伸，何獨劉毅！」

translations.literal: The edict said: “Only consider applying the cord to what truly hits principle—day by day your awe-inspiring wind will extend; why only Liu Yi!”
translations.idiomatic: The edict answered: “See that every case you measure against principle; your authority will grow daily—why cite Liu Yi alone?”

sentences.zh: 時朝廷寬弛，豪右放恣，交私請托，朝野溷淆。

translations.literal: At that time the court was lax and slack; powerful magnates gave free rein, mingling private requests and entrustments; court and countryside were confused.
translations.idiomatic: The court had grown lax; great families traded private favors until court and countryside were a blur.

sentences.zh: 咸奏免河南尹澹、左將軍倩、廷尉高光、兼河南尹何攀等，京都肅然，貴戚懾伏。

translations.literal: Xian memorialized to dismiss the governor of Henan, Dan, the general of the left, Qian, the commandant of justice Gao Guang, concurrent governor of Henan He Pan, and others; the capital was austere, and noble in-laws were awed into submission.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian impeached the governor of Henan (surnamed Dan), the general of the left (surnamed Qian), the commandant of justice Gao Guang, and the concurrent governor of Henan He Pan; the capital grew orderly and the great houses trembled.

sentences.zh: 咸以「聖人久于其道，天下化成。

translations.literal: Xian cited: “When the sage is long on his way, all under Heaven is transformed and completed.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian quoted: “When the sage long pursues his course, the realm is shaped by it.”

sentences.zh: 是以唐、虞三載考績，九年黜陟。

translations.literal: Therefore Tang and Yu examined achievements over three years, promoting and demoting over nine years.
translations.idiomatic: Thus under Tang and Yu officials were graded every three years and promoted or demoted over nine.

sentences.zh: 其在《周禮》，三年大比。

translations.literal: In the *Rites of Zhou*, there is the great comparison every three years.
translations.idiomatic: The *Rites of Zhou* prescribes a great review every three years.”

sentences.zh: 孔子亦云，『三年有成』。

translations.literal: Confucius also said, “In three years there is accomplishment.”
translations.idiomatic: Confucius too said, “Give three years and there will be results.”

sentences.zh: 而中間以來，長吏到官，未幾便遷，百姓困于無定，吏卒疲於送迎」。

translations.literal: Yet in the middle period since then, when senior officers reach their post, before long they are transferred; the hundred surnames are worn out by having no stability, clerks and soldiers exhausted by seeing off and welcoming.”
translations.idiomatic: Yet of late magistrates are shuffled after a short stay; the people suffer endless instability, and runners collapse escorting one chief after another.”

sentences.zh: 時僕射王戎兼吏部，咸奏：「戎備位臺輔，兼掌選舉，不能謐靜風俗，以凝庶績，至令人心傾動，開張浮競。

translations.literal: At that time the vice-director Wang Rong concurrently held the ministry of appointments; Xian memorialized: “Rong occupies a place among ministerial supports and concurrently controls selection; he cannot calm custom and stillness, to coalesce the duties of the many—to the point of letting human hearts tilt and drift, opening and spreading empty rivalry.”
translations.idiomatic: Vice-director Wang Rong then ran the ministry of appointments; Fu Xian charged: “Rong sits among the chief ministers and holds appointments, yet he cannot steady custom or settle administration; hearts waver and empty rivalry spreads.”

sentences.zh: 中郎李重、李義不相匡正。

translations.literal: The gentleman-attendants Li Chong and Li Yi do not correct him.
translations.idiomatic: The gentleman-attendants Li Chong and Li Yi never correct him.”

sentences.zh: 請免戎等官。

translations.literal: I ask that Rong and others be dismissed from office.”
translations.idiomatic: I ask that Wang Rong and his like be removed from office.”

sentences.zh: 」詔曰：「政道之本，誠宜久於其職，咸奏是也。

translations.literal: The edict said: “The root of governing the way truly lies in long tenure in one’s post; what Xian memorialized is right.”
translations.idiomatic: The edict said: “Long tenure is the root of good government; Fu Xian is right.”

sentences.zh: 戎職在論道，吾所崇委，其解禁止。

translations.literal: Rong’s duty lies in discussing the Way—I esteem and entrust him; as for him, dissolve the prohibition.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Rong’s duty is to counsel on the Way, which I value; lift the restrictions on him.”

sentences.zh: 」御史中丞解結以咸劾戎為違典制，越局侵官，干非其分，奏免咸官。

translations.literal: Metropolitan Censor Xie Jie held that Xian’s impeachment of Rong violated canonical regulation, overstepped his office and encroached on another’s duty, meddling beyond his portion, and memorialized to dismiss Xian from office.
translations.idiomatic: Metropolitan censor Xie Jie argued that impeaching Wang Rong broke the rules, overstepped Fu Xian’s charge, and meddled beyond his rank; he asked that Fu Xian be dismissed.

sentences.zh: 詔亦不許。

translations.literal: An edict again did not permit it.
translations.idiomatic: The throne again refused.

sentences.zh: 咸上事以為「按令，御史中丞督司百僚。

translations.literal: Xian submitted a memorial holding: "According to the ordinance, the metropolitan censor supervises the hundred officials."
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian argued in a memorial: "By statute the metropolitan censor supervises every official at court."

sentences.zh: 皇太子以下，其在行馬內，有違法憲者皆彈糾之。

translations.literal: Below the crown prince, those within the mounted patrol corridor who violate statutes are all impeached and investigated.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone from the crown prince downward who breaks the law inside the imperial patrol corridor falls under his impeachment."

sentences.zh: 雖在行馬外，而監司不糾，亦得奏之。

translations.literal: Although outside the mounted corridor, if supervising officials do not impeach, he may still memorialize on them.
translations.idiomatic: Even outside that corridor, if the regional inspectors fail to act, he may still memorialize against them."

sentences.zh: 如令之文，行馬之內有違法憲，謂禁防之事耳。

translations.literal: As the ordinance's wording stands, violations of statutes within the mounted corridor refer to matters of forbidden-precinct security alone.
translations.idiomatic: The statute’s wording ties the corridor to palace security alone."

sentences.zh: 宮內禁防，外司不得而行，故專施中丞。

translations.literal: Forbidden precincts inside the palace—outside agencies may not act therein—therefore authority is vested solely in the central censor.
translations.idiomatic: Inner-palace security is closed to outside bureaus, which is why the metropolitan censor alone holds that beat."

sentences.zh: 今道路橋梁不修，鬥訟屠沽不絕，如此之比，中丞推責州坐，即今所謂行馬內語施於禁防。

translations.literal: Now roads and bridges are not repaired, brawls and butchers and peddlers do not cease—such cases: the censor presses blame on the province to sit—then what is now called 'within the mounted corridor' language is applied to security matters.
translations.idiomatic: Neglected roads, endless lawsuits, unruly markets—the censor blames the province, yet people now stretch the phrase ‘inside the corridor’ to cover such civic ills."

sentences.zh: 既雲中丞督司百僚矣，何復說行馬之內乎！

translations.literal: Since it already says the central censor supervises the hundred officials, why again speak of 'within the mounted corridor'!
translations.idiomatic: If the censor already oversees all officials, why narrow him again to the corridor?"

sentences.zh: 既雲百僚，而不得復說行馬之內者，內外眾官謂之百僚，則通內外矣。

translations.literal: Since it says 'hundred officials,' yet may not again speak of 'within the mounted corridor'—the many officials inside and out are called the hundred officials, then it comprehends inside and outside.
translations.idiomatic: The ‘hundred officials’ means everyone at court and in the provinces—inside and outside together."

sentences.zh: 司隸所以不復說行馬內外者，禁防之事已於中丞說之故也。

translations.literal: The reason the colonel director of retainers does not again speak of inside or outside the mounted corridor is that security matters were already stated with regard to the central censor.
translations.idiomatic: The colonel director omits the corridor because the censor’s statute already covers palace security."

sentences.zh: 中丞、司隸俱糾皇太子以下，則共對司內外矣，不為中丞專司內百僚，司隸專司外百僚。

translations.literal: Central censor and colonel director of retainers together impeach from the crown prince downward, then they jointly face duties inside and outside—it is not that the central censor solely supervises inner hundred officials and the colonel solely outer hundred officials.
translations.idiomatic: Censor and colonel both impeach from the crown prince down; they share inner and outer duty—it is not a split between two separate rosters."

sentences.zh: 自有中丞、司隸以來，更互奏內外眾官，惟所糾得無內外之限也。

translations.literal: From the time there have been central censor and colonel director of retainers, they have alternately memorialized on many officials inside and out—only when impeaching there is no inside-outside limit.
translations.idiomatic: Since both offices were created they have taken turns impeaching officials everywhere, with no hard line between inner and outer."

sentences.zh: 而結一旦橫挫臣，臣前所以不羅縷者，冀因結奏得從私願也。

translations.literal: Yet Jie in one morning harshly thwarted your subject; the reason your subject earlier did not belabor detail was that I hoped through Jie's memorial my private wish might be granted.
translations.idiomatic: Xie Jie suddenly blocked me; I had not argued every clause because I hoped his memorial would win me the ruling I sought."

sentences.zh: 今既所願不從，而敕雲但為過耳，非所不及也，以此見原。

translations.literal: Now since what was wished is not followed, yet the edict says it was only excess, not what one could not reach, and by this pardons me.
translations.idiomatic: Now my request is denied, yet the edict calls it a mere excess—not something beyond my duty—and forgives me on that ground."

sentences.zh: 臣忝司直之任，宜當正己率人，若其有過，不敢受原，是以申陳其愚。

translations.literal: Your subject disgraces the duty of director of correctness—ought to rectify self and lead others; if there is fault, I dare not accept pardon—therefore I declare this foolishness.
translations.idiomatic: I hold the post of censor-in-chief: I must set the example. If I was wrong I should not be excused, so I lay out my reasoning bluntly."

sentences.zh: 司隸與中丞俱共糾皇太子以下，則從皇太子以下無所不糾也。

translations.literal: When colonel director of retainers and central censor together impeach from the crown prince down, then from the crown prince down there is nothing they do not impeach.
translations.idiomatic: If censor and colonel both impeach from the crown prince downward, nothing below that rank lies outside their reach."

sentences.zh: 得糾皇太子而不得糾尚書，臣之暗塞既所未譬。

translations.literal: To be able to impeach the crown prince yet not be able to impeach the director of the secretariat—your subject's dim obstruction I have never grasped the parallel.
translations.idiomatic: I may impeach the heir yet not the secretariat director—this blind spot I cannot understand."

sentences.zh: 皇太子為在行馬之內邪，皇太子在行馬之內而得糾之，尚書在行馬之內而不得糾，無有此理。

translations.literal: Is the crown prince inside the mounted corridor or not? If the crown prince inside the mounted corridor may be impeached, yet the director of the secretariat inside the mounted corridor may not be impeached—there is no such principle.
translations.idiomatic: Is the heir inside the corridor or not? If the heir inside may be impeached but the secretariat director inside may not, that rule does not exist."

sentences.zh: 此理灼然，而結以此挫臣。

translations.literal: This principle is glaringly clear, yet Jie for this thwarted your subject.
translations.idiomatic: The logic is obvious, yet Xie Jie used it to block me."

sentences.zh: 臣可無恨耳，其於觀聽，無乃有怪邪！

translations.literal: Your subject may have no resentment—but for those who look and listen, is it not strange!
translations.idiomatic: I can swallow the insult—but will not the world find it absurd?"

sentences.zh: 臣識石公前在殿上脫衣，為司隸荀愷所奏，先帝不以為非，于時莫謂侵官；

translations.literal: Your subject remembers when Lord Shi bared his torso in the hall, impeached by colonel director Xun Kai—the late emperor did not think it wrong; at the time none said it encroached on office;
translations.idiomatic: I recall when Lord Shi stripped in the hall and Xun Kai impeached him—the late emperor approved, and no one cried ‘overreach.’"

sentences.zh: 今臣裁糾尚書，而當有罪乎？

translations.literal: now when your subject only impeached the director of the secretariat, should there be guilt?
translations.idiomatic: Am I now to be punished for impeaching only the secretariat director?"

sentences.zh: 」咸累自上稱引故事，條理灼然，朝廷無以易之。

translations.literal: " Xian repeatedly cited himself to superior, adducing precedents; the ordering was clear and the court had no way to change it.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Xian piled precedent on precedent until the case was airtight and the court could not refute him.

sentences.zh: 吳郡顧榮常與親故書曰：「傅長虞為司隸，勁直忠果，劾按驚人。

translations.literal: Gu Rong of Wu commandery often wrote to kinsmen and old friends, saying: "Fu Changyu as colonel director of retainers was forceful, straight, loyal, and resolute; his impeachments and investigations startled men.
translations.idiomatic: Gu Rong of Wu often wrote to friends that Fu Xian as colonel director was fierce, loyal, and fearless—his indictments shook the capital."

sentences.zh: 雖非周才，偏亮可貴也。

translations.literal: Though not all-round talent, his partial brilliance is precious.
translations.idiomatic: He was not a universal genius, but his moral brilliance was rare."

sentences.zh: 」卒官，時年五十六，詔贈司隸校尉，朝服一具、衣一襲、錢二十萬，諡曰貞。

translations.literal: " He died in office at age fifty-six; an edict posthumously awarded him the title colonel director of retainers, one set of court dress, one suit of clothes, two hundred thousand cash, posthumous name Zhen.
translations.idiomatic: He died in office at fifty-six. The court posthumously restored his colonel’s title, gave court dress, a suit, two hundred thousand cash, and the posthumous name Zhen, ‘the steadfast.’"

sentences.zh: 有三子：敷、晞、纂。

translations.literal: He had three sons: Fu, Xi, and Zuan.
translations.idiomatic: He left three sons: Fu, Xi, and Zuan.

sentences.zh: 長子敷嗣。

translations.literal: The eldest son Fu inherited.
translations.idiomatic: The eldest son, Fu, inherited his title.

sentences.zh: 敷字穎根，清靜有道，素解屬文。

translations.literal: Fu's style name was Yingen; he was pure, quiet, and possessed the Way, by nature skilled at composing texts.
translations.idiomatic: Fu, courtesy name Yingen, was serene, reclusive, and a gifted writer.

sentences.zh: 除太子舍人，轉尚書郎、太傅參軍，皆不起。

translations.literal: He was appointed attendant to the heir apparent, transferred to gentleman of the secretariat and aide to the grand tutor, but on each occasion did not take up office.
translations.idiomatic: He was named attendant to the heir apparent, then secretary and staff officer to the grand tutor, but declined each post.

sentences.zh: 永嘉之亂，避地會稽，元帝引為鎮東從事中郎。

translations.literal: In the Yongjia turmoil he fled to Kuaiji; Yuan-di summoned him as aide-de-camp on the staff of the general who garrisons the east.
translations.idiomatic: When Yongjia brought chaos he fled to Kuaiji; Prince Langya (later Yuan-di) summoned him as aide on the staff of the general who guards the east.

sentences.zh: 素有贏疾，頻見敦喻，辭不獲免，輿病到職。

translations.literal: By nature he had a wasting illness; repeatedly he was urged yet declined and could not escape; he took up duty sick in a litter.
translations.idiomatic: Chronic illness had long wasted him; though he begged off, he could not refuse and arrived in a sickbed litter to take office.

sentences.zh: 數月卒，時年四十六。

translations.literal: Before several months he died at age forty-six.
translations.idiomatic: Within months he was dead at forty-six.

sentences.zh: 晞亦有才思，為上虞令，甚有政績，卒于司徒西曹屬。

translations.literal: Xi too had talent and thought; he was magistrate of Shangyu with very good administrative record, dying as an aide in the western bureau of the minister of education.
translations.idiomatic: Xi was also clever and thoughtful; as magistrate of Shangyu he earned praise for good rule, and died as an aide in the minister of education’s western bureau.

sentences.zh: 傅祗

translations.literal: Fu Zhi.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Zhi

sentences.zh: 祗字子莊。

translations.literal: Zhi's style name was Zizhuang.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Zhi, courtesy name Zizhuang.

sentences.zh: 父嘏，魏太常。

translations.literal: His father was Gu, grand master of ceremonies of Wei.
translations.idiomatic: His father, Fu Gu, had been grand master of ceremonies under the Wei.

sentences.zh: 祗性至孝，早知名，以才識明練稱。

translations.literal: Zhi by nature was utmost filial, early known by name, praised for talent, insight, clarity, and experience.
translations.idiomatic: Deeply filial and famous early, he was admired for shrewd, seasoned ability.

sentences.zh: 武帝始建東宮，起家太子舍人，累遷散騎黃門郎，賜爵關內侯，食邑三百戶。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu of Jin first built the eastern palace, on leaving mourning he became attendant to the heir apparent; by stages he was promoted to cavalier attendant and gentleman at the yellow gate, enfeoffed secondary marquis within the passes with three hundred households' income.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Jin founded the heir’s palace, Fu Zhi left mourning to become an heir’s attendant, rose to cavalier attendant and gentleman at the yellow gate, and received a secondary marquisate within the passes with three hundred households.

sentences.zh: 母憂去職。

translations.literal: On his mother's bereavement he left office.
translations.idiomatic: He resigned to mourn his mother.

sentences.zh: 及葬母，詔給太常五等吉凶導從。

translations.literal: When burying his mother, an edict granted the grand master of ceremonies the five-grade auspicious and inauspicious escort squads.
translations.idiomatic: For her burial the court ordered the grand master of ceremonies to supply the full five-grade funeral escort.

sentences.zh: 其後諸卿夫人葬給導從，自此始也。

translations.literal: Afterwards when ministers' wives were buried they were given escort squads—this began here.
translations.idiomatic: Later, when ministers’ wives were buried, they too received such escorts—the practice began with him.

sentences.zh: 服終，為滎陽太守。

translations.literal: When mourning ended he became governor of Xingyang.
translations.idiomatic: When mourning ended he became governor of Xingyang.

sentences.zh: 自魏黃初大水之後，河濟泛溢，鄧艾嘗著《濟河論》，開石門而通之，至是復浸壞。
